kcet|Mathematics|2018|6|MTG Karnataka-CE:
Each handshake involves **two** people, and each pair shakes hands exactly once. So the
number of handshakes is the number of **ways of choosing 2 people from n** — a combination,
not a permutation, since a handshake between P and Q is the same as one between Q and P.
**Step 1 — set up the equation.**
C(n, 2) = 45
n(n − 1)/2 = 45
**n(n − 1) = 90**
**Step 2 — solve.** Look for two consecutive integers whose product is 90:
9 × 10 = 90 ✓
so **n = 10**
(Formally: n² − n − 90 = 0, which factorises as (n − 10)(n + 9) = 0, giving n = 10 or
n = −9. The negative root is discarded, since a number of people cannot be negative.)
**Check:** with 10 people, C(10, 2) = 10 × 9/2 = **45** ✓
The distractor to watch is **(a) 9**: it is tempting because 9 × 10 = 90 appears in the
working, and because each person shakes hands with 9 others. But 10 people each shaking 9
hands counts every handshake **twice**, giving 10 × 9/2 = 45 — the division by 2 is exactly
what makes the answer 10 rather than 9.
The same combinatorial count answers a family of questions: the number of lines through n
points (no three collinear), the number of diagonals plus sides of an n-gon, and the number
of matches in a round-robin tournament are all C(n, 2).
∴ 10.
kcet|Mathematics|2014|1|MTG Karnataka-CE:
Start from the definition of conditional probability:
**P(B/A) = P(A ∩ B) / P(A)**, valid since P(A) ≠ 0
**Case (i) — A is a subset of B.**
If every outcome of A lies in B, then A ∩ B is the whole of A:
**A ∩ B = A**
so
P(B/A) = P(A)/P(A) = **1**
In words: given that A has happened, B is **certain**, because A happening guarantees B.
**Case (ii) — A ∩ B = φ** (the events are mutually exclusive).
The intersection is empty, so
P(A ∩ B) = P(φ) = 0
and therefore
P(B/A) = 0/P(A) = **0**
In words: given that A has happened, B is **impossible**, because the two cannot occur
together.
So the two answers in order are **1, 0** ✓ — option (d).
The two cases are the extremes of conditional probability, and knowing them is a useful
sanity check on any such calculation: P(B/A) must always lie between 0 and 1, reaching 1
when A forces B and 0 when A excludes it.
The order matters — option (b), 0, 1, is the same pair reversed, and reading which case is
(i) and which is (ii) is half the question.
∴ 1, 0.
kcet|Mathematics|2014|2|MTG Karnataka-CE:
**Step 1 — count the sample space.** Two dice, each with 6 faces, give
6 × 6 = **36** equally likely outcomes
(and they must be treated as **ordered** pairs, since the dice are distinguishable).
**Step 2 — list the favourable outcomes.** The pairs totalling 5 are
(1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 1)
that is **4** outcomes. Note that (1, 4) and (4, 1) are **different** outcomes and both
count — overlooking that is the commonest error here.
**Step 3 — the probability.**
P = 4/36 = **1/9** ✓
The trap is treating {1, 4} and {2, 3} as just **two** unordered combinations, which would
give 2/36 = 1/18 — option (b), placed there for exactly that mistake. Because the two dice
are separate objects, the order is real and each unordered pair of **different** numbers
corresponds to **two** outcomes.
A useful cross-check is the symmetry of dice totals. The number of ways of making each total
runs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 for totals 2 to 12 — so a total of 5 has **4** ways ✓
and the probabilities sum to 36/36 = 1 as they must.
Note also that a total of 5 can only be made from **unequal** numbers (since 5 is odd), so
every one of its combinations doubles — which is why the count is even.
∴ 1/9.
kcet|Mathematics|2014|4|MTG Karnataka-CE:
The box has 100 bulbs of which **10 are defective** and **90 are good**, so the probability
that any one bulb drawn is good is
90/100 = **9/10**
**Treating the draws as independent**, which is the intention here, the probability that
all five are good is
(9/10) × (9/10) × (9/10) × (9/10) × (9/10) = **(9/10)⁵** ✓
This is the **binomial** model: five independent trials, each with probability p = 9/10 of
success, and the required probability is p⁵ with no combinatorial factor, since there is
only one way for all five to be good.
(9/10)⁵ ≈ 0·59, so a little under three times in five the sample is clean.
Why the others are wrong:
**(a) 9/10** is the probability for a **single** bulb, not five.
**(b) (1/10)⁵** is the probability that **all five are defective** — the complementary
extreme.
**(d) (1/2)⁵** uses a probability of 1/2 per bulb, which the data do not support.
A remark on exactness: strictly the bulbs are drawn **without** replacement, so the precise
answer is C(90,5)/C(100,5) ≈ 0·583. With 100 bulbs the difference from (9/10)⁵ = 0·590 is
under 1 %, and the question's options show it expects the simpler independent model.
∴ (9/10)⁵.

kcet|Mathematics|2006|2|MTG Karnataka-CE:
Work out the two sets separately, then form the Cartesian product.
**Step 1 — the difference A − B.** This is the elements of A that are **not** in B.
A = {a, b, c}, B = {b, c, d}
b and c are in B, so they go; a is not, so it stays:
**A − B = {a}**
**Step 2 — the intersection B ∩ C.** The elements in **both**.
B = {b, c, d}, C = {a, d, c}
b is not in C; c is in both ✓; d is in both ✓:
**B ∩ C = {c, d}**
**Step 3 — the Cartesian product.** Every ordered pair with the first element from A − B and
the second from B ∩ C:
{a} × {c, d} = **{(a, c), (a, d)}** ✓
**Check the size:** |A − B| × |B ∩ C| = 1 × 2 = **2** pairs ✓ as found.
The **order** within each pair matters, and it follows the order of the product: the first
set supplies the first coordinate. Option (c), {(c, a), (d, a)}, is the product taken the
other way round — that is (B ∩ C) × (A − B) — and is the main trap.
Option (d) adds (b, d), which would require b to be in A − B; but b belongs to B, so it was
removed at step 1.
∴ {(a, c), (a, d)}.

kcet|Mathematics|2006|3|MTG Karnataka-CE.s:
The function must be **one-one** (injective) but **not onto** (not surjective), so the domain
must be a stretch on which sin is strictly monotonic, and the codomain must be **bigger**
than the range.
Test each pair.
**(a) R and R** ✗ — sin is **not one-one** on R (sin 0 = sin π = 0), and its range is only
[−1, 1], so it is not onto either. It fails the first requirement.
**(b) [0, π] and [0, 1]** ✗ — on [0, π] the sine rises then falls, so it is **not one-one**:
sin(π/6) = sin(5π/6) = 1/2.
**(d) [−π/2, π/2] and [−1, 1]** ✗ — sine **is** one-one here, increasing throughout. But its
range over this interval is exactly **[−1, 1]**, so it is **onto** as well. This is the
standard bijective restriction used to define sin⁻¹ — and the question asks for a function
that is *not* onto.
**(c) [0, π/2] and [−1, 1]** ✓ — sine is increasing on [0, π/2], so it is **one-one**. But
its range there is only **[0, 1]**, which is a proper subset of the codomain [−1, 1]:
nothing maps to any negative value. So it is **not onto** ✓
Both conditions are met, and only by (c).
The pair (c) and (d) is the heart of the question: they differ only in the domain, and that
difference is exactly what turns a bijection into an injection that misses half its
codomain.
∴ [0, π/2] and [−1, 1].

Note: the printed key gives (d), but on [−π/2, π/2] the sine takes every value in [−1, 1],
so it **is** onto there. The key is wrong and has been corrected to (c).

kcet|Mathematics|2011|14|MTG Karnataka-C:
Test each property on A = {1, 2, 3, 4} with xRy meaning **x divides y**.
**Reflexive?** Is xRx for every x — that is, does every number divide itself?
1|1, 2|2, 3|3, 4|4 ✓ **yes, reflexive**
**Symmetric?** If xRy must yRx follow — that is, if x divides y, does y divide x?
Take x = 1, y = 2: **1 divides 2** ✓ but **2 does not divide 1** ✗
So **not symmetric**
**Transitive?** If x divides y and y divides z, does x divide z?
Yes, always: if y = xk and z = ym then z = x(km), so x divides z ✓ **transitive**
(Example in this set: 1|2 and 2|4, and indeed 1|4 ✓)
So the relation is **reflexive and transitive** ✓ — option (a).
It is **not an equivalence relation**, since equivalence requires all three properties, and
symmetry fails — so option (d) is out.
A relation that is reflexive, transitive and **antisymmetric** (as this one is: if x|y and
y|x then x = y) is called a **partial order**. Divisibility is the standard example, and it
is 'partial' precisely because not every pair is comparable — 2 and 3 divide neither one
another.
Written out, R = {(1,1), (1,2), (1,3), (1,4), (2,2), (2,4), (3,3), (4,4)} — eight pairs, with
all four reflexive ones present and no pair reversed.
∴ reflexive and transitive.
kcet|Mathematics|2012|18|MTG Karnataka-C:
First check that the inverse exists at all, then find it.
**Step 1 — is f a bijection?** f(x) = 2x + 3 is a straight line with non-zero gradient, so
**one-one:** if 2x₁ + 3 = 2x₂ + 3 then x₁ = x₂ ✓
**onto:** for any y in R, solving y = 2x + 3 gives a real x ✓
So f is a bijection and f⁻¹ exists — which disposes of options (a) and (d) at once.
**Step 2 — find the inverse.** Put y = f(x) and solve for x:
y = 2x + 3
y − 3 = 2x
x = (y − 3)/2
**Step 3 — rename the variable.** Writing the inverse as a function of x:
**f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2** ✓
**Check:** f(f⁻¹(x)) = 2·(x − 3)/2 + 3 = (x − 3) + 3 = **x** ✓ and
f⁻¹(f(x)) = (2x + 3 − 3)/2 = **x** ✓ both ways, as an inverse must.
The trap is option (c), 1/(2x + 3), which is the **reciprocal** of f, not its inverse. The
notation f⁻¹ for an inverse **function** and x⁻¹ for a reciprocal **number** look alike and
mean quite different things: f⁻¹ undoes f, whereas 1/f(x) does not.
The method generalises: to invert any bijection, write y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y,
and then swap the names of the variables.
∴ (x − 3)/2.
